## TL;DR  
Yes – you can serve **static** map tiles (XYZ raster tiles or XYZ/PMTiles vector tiles) directly from a GitHub Pages site and use them with MapLibre GL JS.  
What you **cannot** do on GitHub Pages is run a dynamic tile server (e.g. TileServer‑GL, TileStache, etc.) – the platform only serves files that already exist in the repository.  

Below is a complete, step‑by‑step guide that shows:

1. **What kinds of tiles work on a static host**  
2. **How to prepare the tiles and the style JSON**  
3. **How to make GitHub Pages serve the correct MIME types (especially for vector tiles)**  
4. **How to load the tiles in MapLibre GL JS**  
5. **Practical limits & work‑arounds** (repo size, bandwidth, caching, alternatives).

---

## 1. What “static‑only” means for map tiles

| Tile type | How it’s stored | How it’s served on GitHub Pages | Typical use case |
|----------|----------------|--------------------------------|------------------|
| **Raster XYZ** (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.webp`) | Folder hierarchy `/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | Served as ordinary image files – no special handling needed. | Basemaps, satellite imagery, DEM hillshades. |
| **Vector XYZ** (`.pbf`) | Same hierarchy `/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` | Needs the correct `Content‑Type: application/x-protobuf` header. GitHub Pages can be told to use this MIME type via a `.gitattributes` file. | Vector‑tile basemaps, custom data layers. |
| **PMTiles** (`.pmtiles`) | Single file (or a few files) | Served as a binary blob (`application/octet-stream`). MapLibre can read it directly if you use the `pmtiles` protocol (`pmtiles://…`). | Very compact distribution of whole tile sets (good for small‑to‑medium projects). |
| **Other formats** (`.json`, `.geojson`, `.mvt`, …) | Same as above | Same approach – just make sure the MIME type is correct. | Data layers, style files, sprite sheets. |

> **Bottom line:** Anything that can be represented as a file on disk can be served by GitHub Pages. The only extra step is to make sure the browser receives the right `Content‑Type` header for non‑image files.

---

## 2. Preparing the tile set

### 2.1. Choose a tile format

| When to use | Recommended format |
|-------------|--------------------|
| Small‑ish basemap (≤ 200 MB) that you want to keep in a single file | **PMTiles** (easiest to version, only one file). |
| Larger basemap or you already have an XYZ folder structure | **XYZ raster** (`.png/.jpg`) **or** **XYZ vector** (`.pbf`). |
| You need to serve many layers from the same repository (e.g., separate folders for roads, landuse) | **XYZ vector** (folder per layer) – still static. |

### 2.2. Generating the tiles

| Tool | Output | Command example |
|------|--------|-----------------|
| **Tippecanoe** (vector) | `tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` | `tippecanoe -o tiles.pmtiles -zg --drop-densest --no-tile-size-limit mydata.geojson` (PMTiles) |
| **gdal2tiles.py** (raster) | `tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | `gdal2tiles.py -z 0-14 -r bilinear my.tif tiles/` |
| **MapTiler** (GUI) | XYZ raster or vector | `maptiler -i my.tif -o tiles/ --format png` |
| **mbutil** (extract from MBTiles) | XYZ folder | `mb-util mytiles.mbtiles tiles/` |

> **Tip:** Keep the folder depth shallow (e.g., `tiles/10/523/391.pbf`) – GitHub Pages can handle deep hierarchies, but the Git index becomes slower the more files you have. For > 10 k tiles per zoom level consider **PMTiles** instead.

### 2.3. Add the tiles to your repo

```
my‑map‑repo/
├─ index.html                # your page that loads MapLibre
├─ style.json                # MapLibre style referencing the tiles
├─ tiles/
│  ├─ 0/
│  │  └─ 0/
│  │     └─ 0.png
│  ├─ 1/
│  │  └─ …
│  └─ …
└─ .gitattributes           # MIME‑type overrides (see next section)
```

Commit everything (GitHub allows up to **1 GB** per repository, **100 MB** per file). If you exceed those limits you’ll need a different host (see §5).

## 3. Making GitHub Pages serve the right MIME types

GitHub Pages uses the **GitHub Pages static file server** (based on Jekyll). By default it guesses MIME types from the file extension, but for some extensions (especially `.pbf`) it falls back to `application/octet-stream`. Below is a **step‑by‑step cheat‑sheet** you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or a short script) to:

1. **Inspect the PMTiles archive** – see the metadata that tells you which vector‑tile layers are inside.  
2. **Validate the file** – make sure the header, index and tile data are all well‑formed.  
3. **Optionally extract a single tile** and decode it so you can double‑check the layer names and feature fields.

Everything works on Linux, macOS, or Windows (Subsystem for Linux works just as well).  
You only need a couple of tiny command‑line tools (Node‑based) or a short Python script – no heavy GIS software required.

---

## 1️⃣ Install the official PMTiles command‑line tools

The easiest way is the **npm** package that ships the `pmtiles` binary.

```bash
# If you already have Node.js (>=14) installed:
npm install -g @mapbox/pmtiles-cli
# The binary will be called `pmtiles`
# Verify it installed:
pmtiles --version
```

*If you prefer Python, you can also `pip install pmtiles` – the library provides the same API, but the CLI is a bit more convenient for quick checks.*

---

## 2️⃣ Quick “what’s inside?” – read the metadata

```bash
pmtiles info my‑tiles.pmtiles
```

Typical output (truncated for brevity):

```
{
  "version": 3,
  "root_dir": "tiles",
  "tile_type": "pbf",
  "max_zoom": 14,
  "min_zoom": 0,
  "center": [12.4924,41.8902,12],
  "bounds": [12.0,41.5,13.0,42.0],
  "metadata": {
    "json": {
      "vector_layers": [
        {
          "id": "roads",
          "description": "Road network",
          "fields": {"class":"String","name":"String"}
        },
        {
          "id": "buildings",
          "description": "Building footprints",
          "fields": {"height":"Number","name":"String"}
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

*The `vector_layers` array is the definitive list of layers that the PMTiles file contains.*  
If you don’t see a `vector_layers` entry, the file probably contains raster tiles (or the metadata was never written).  

### What to look for

| Item | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|
| `version` | Should be `3` (current spec). Anything else means you’re using an old spec – still readable but worth updating. |
| `tile_type` | `"pbf"` = vector tiles, `"png"`/`"jpg"` = raster. |
| `max_zoom` / `min_zoom` | Confirm they match what you intended when you generated the file. |
| `metadata.json.vector_layers` | The list of layer IDs and their field definitions. This is what you’ll use in a style or when you query the tiles. |
| `bounds` / `center` | Geographic envelope – useful for sanity‑checking that the tiles cover the area you expect. |

---

## 3️⃣ Full validation – check the file structure

The CLI ships a **`validate`** sub‑command that runs the same checks the PMTiles server does when it opens a file.

```bash
pmtiles validate my‑tiles.pmtiles
```

Possible outcomes:

| Result | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `✅ OK – header, index and all tiles are consistent` | The file is structurally sound and ready to be served. |
| `❌ ERROR: Invalid header magic bytes` | The file is not a PMTiles archive (maybe you passed an MBTiles file by mistake). |
| `❌ ERROR: Tile offset out of bounds` | The internal index points to a location that doesn’t exist – the file is corrupted. |
| `❌ ERROR: Tile data checksum mismatch` | The tile payload is damaged (e.g., truncated download). |

If you get any error, regenerate the PMTiles file (or run a repair tool – see the “Repair” section below).

---

## 4️⃣ Optional: Pull a single tile and decode it locally

Sometimes you want to **see the actual layer names** that appear inside a tile, especially if the metadata is missing or you suspect a bug.

```bash
# Grab tile z=0, x=0, y=0 (the top‑left tile of the whole dataset)
pmtiles tile my‑tiles.pmtiles 0 0 0 > tile-0-0-0.pbf
```

Now decode the protobuf with a tiny Node or Python script.

### 4a. Node (using `@mapbox/vector-tile`)

```bash
npm install -g @mapbox/vector-tile
node - <<'NODE'
const fs = require('fs');
const { VectorTile } = require('@mapbox/vector-tile');
const Protobuf = require('pbf');

const data = fs.readFileSync('tile-0-0-0.pbf');
const tile = new VectorTile(new Protobuf(data));

console.log('Layers in this tile:');
for (const layerName of Object.keys(tile.layers)) {
  const layer = tile.layers[layerName];
  console.log(`- ${layerName} (features: ${layer.length})`);
}
NODE
```

### 4b. Python (using `mapbox-vector-tile`)

```bash
pip install mapbox-vector-tile
python - <<'PY'
import json, sys
from mapbox_vector_tile import decode

with open('tile-0-0-0.pbf', 'rb') as f:
    tile = decode(f.read())

print('Layers in this tile:')
for layer_name, features in tile.items():
    print(f'- {layer_name} (features: {len(features)})')
PY
```

You should see the same layer IDs that appeared in the `vector_layers` metadata. If they differ, the metadata is out‑of‑date – regenerate the PMTiles with proper metadata (most tools have a flag like `--metadata` or `--layer-names`).

---

## 5️⃣ Quick “repair” if validation fails

If `pmtiles validate` reports a problem, you can often fix it without a full re‑run:

```bash
# Re‑write the index (useful when the index got corrupted but tiles are fine)
pmtiles rebuild-index my‑tiles.pmtiles
# Then validate again
pmtiles validate my‑tiles.pmtiles
```

If the index rebuild still fails, the safest route is to **re‑create the PMTiles** from the source data (GeoJSON, Shapefile, etc.) using the same tool you used originally (e.g., `tippecanoe`, `ogr2ogr`, `pmtiles convert`).

---

## 6️⃣ Putting it all together – a one‑liner script

If you want a single command that **(a)** prints the layer list, **(b)** validates the file, and **(c)** exits with a non‑zero status on any problem, try this Bash snippet:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

FILE=$1

# 1️⃣ Print layers (or “no layers”)
echo "🔎  Inspecting $FILE …"
LAYERS=$(pmtiles info "$FILE" | jq -r '.metadata.json.vector_layers[].id' 2>/dev/null || true)
if [[ -z $LAYERS ]]; then
  echo "⚠️  No vector_layers metadata found – maybe a raster PMTiles?"
else
  echo "🗂  Vector layers:"
  echo "$LAYERS" | sed 's/^/   • /'
fi

# 2️⃣ Validate
echo "✅  Running structural validation…"
pmtiles validate "$FILE"
echo "✅  Validation passed!"

# 3️⃣ (optional) quick tile check – sample the centre tile
Z=$(pmtiles info "$FILE" | jq -r '.max_zoom')
X=$(pmtiles info "$FILE" | jq -r '.bounds[0]')   # just a placeholder; you can compute a real centre tile if you like
Y=$(pmtiles info "$FILE" | jq -r '.bounds[1]')

# (skip if you don't need it)
# pmtiles tile "$FILE" $Z $X $Y > /dev/null

echo "🎉  $FILE looks good – ready to upload!"
```

Save as `check-pmtiles.sh`, `chmod +x check-pmtiles.sh`, then run:

```bash
./check-pmtiles.sh my-tiles.pmtiles
```

The script will exit with status **0** only if validation succeeds; any error bubbles up as a non‑zero exit code, which is handy for CI pipelines.

---

## 7️⃣ TL;DR – The minimal commands you need

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **List layers** | `pmtiles info my.pmtiles \| jq '.metadata.json.vector_layers[].id'` |
| **Validate file** | `pmtiles validate my.pmtiles` |
| **Extract a tile** | `pmtiles tile my.pmtiles 0 0 0 > tile.pbf` |
| **Decode tile (Node)** | `node -e "const {VectorTile}=require('@mapbox/vector-tile'); const Protobuf=require('pbf'); const fs=require('fs'); const t=new VectorTile(new Protobuf(fs.readFileSync('tile.pbf'))); console.log(Object.keys(t.layers));"` |
| **Decode tile (Python)** | `python -c "import json; from mapbox_vector_tile import decode; print(json.dumps(list(decode(open('tile.pbf','rb').read()).keys()), indent=2))"` |

---

## 8️⃣ What to do **before uploading** to a tile server

1. **Run the validation** (`pmtiles validate`).  
2. **Confirm the layer list** matches the style you’ll use (e.g., `roads`, `buildings`).  
3. **Check the geographic envelope** (`pmtiles info … .bounds`) – it should intersect the area you intend to serve.  
4. **Compute a checksum** (optional but nice for integrity checks):  

   ```bash
   sha256sum my.pmtiles > my.pmtiles.sha256
   ```

5. **Upload** – most cloud providers (e.g., AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Azure Blob) accept the file as‑is; just make sure the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/octet-stream` or `application/vnd.pmtiles` (the latter is the official MIME type).

---

| Resource | Link |
|----------|------|
| PMTiles spec (v3) | <https://github.com/protomaps/PMTiles/blob/main/spec/v3/spec.md> |
| Official CLI repo | <https://github.com/protomaps/PMTiles/tree/main/cli> |
| Node library (`@mapbox/pmtiles`) | <https://github.com/protomaps/PMTiles/tree/main/js> |

| Quick viewer (no‑install) | <https://pmtiles.io/> – drag‑and‑drop a `.pmtiles` file and explore layers in the browser. |

Run the commands above, verify the layer list and the structural integrity, and you can upload the PMTiles with confidence that the server (or CDN) will serve exactly what you expect. If anything looks off, regenerate the archive with the proper `--metadata`/`--layer` flags from your source data, and re‑run the checks. Happy tiling!

**Short answer:**  
The PMTiles loader only works when the archive is given to the map via the **`url`** property (or via a `pmtiles://` source object). Supplying a `tiles` array that contains a template like `pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}` is not supported – the map will try to fetch tiles the way it does for ordinary HTTP raster/vector sources, and the PMTiles protocol handler will not be invoked for the higher‑zoom requests. The result is a series of “blank” tiles even though the archive itself contains data for those zoom levels (as you can see with `pmtiles show`).

Below is a more detailed walk‑through of why this happens and how to fix it.

---

## 1. What the `tiles` array is for

In MapLibre GL JS / Mapbox GL JS a **`tiles`** array is meant for *explicit* tile URLs, e.g.

```json
{
  "type": "raster",
  "tiles": [
    "https://my.cdn.com/tiles/0/0/0.png",
    "https://my.cdn.com/tiles/0/0/1.png",
    …
  ]
}
```

If you give a *template* (`…/{z}/{x}/{y}`) the library will **replace** the placeholders **itself** and then issue a normal `fetch()` request for each tile. The request goes straight to the network stack; no special protocol handler (like the one that understands `pmtiles://`) is consulted.

Because the request is a plain HTTP GET, the PMTiles loader never sees it, and the request fails (usually with a 404). At low zoom levels you may still see something because the map falls back to the “fallback tile” that the source may have defined, but as soon as you go past the zoom where the fallback is used, you get blank tiles.

---

## 2. Why it looks like it works at low zooms

* **Fallback tiles** – many vector‑tile sources have a built‑in “empty” tile that is returned when the loader cannot find a tile. This is why you still see something at zooms 0‑5, for example.
* **Cache / pre‑loaded tiles** – if you have previously loaded the same tile from another source (e.g., a regular XYZ URL) the browser may serve it from cache, masking the problem until you request a tile that has never been cached.

None of this means the PMTiles archive is being read; it’s just the map’s normal error‑handling.

---

## 3. The correct way to use a PMTiles archive

### 3.1. Use the `url` property (the simplest)

```json
{
  "id": "my-pmtiles",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/tiles/my‑tiles.pmtiles",
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "minzoom": 0
}
```

* The `pmtiles://` scheme tells the PMTiles loader to open the archive, read its internal tile index, and serve the appropriate tile data for any `{z}/{x}/{y}` request that the map makes.
* The loader automatically respects the `maxzoom`/`minzoom` that are stored in the archive’s metadata. If you want to override them, you can add them to the source definition (they will be merged with the archive’s values).

### 3.2. If you really need a `tiles` array

You can still provide a `tiles` array, **but it must contain concrete URLs**, not a template. For a PMTiles archive that would look like:

```json

  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": [
    "pmtiles://https://example.com/tiles/my‑tiles.pmtiles/0/0/0",
    "pmtiles://https://example.com/tiles/my‑tiles.pmtiles/0/0/1",
    …
  ]
}
```

Generating that list manually is impractical, which is why the `url` property exists in the first place. In short: *don’t use a template in a `tiles` array*.
